The first thing I notice is the light. It doesn’t arrive all at once; it leaks through the blinds in thin, pale bands, testing the floorboards before it commits. I sit with coffee that is already too cool, and I watch dust move in the slanted sunbeam like tiny planets in a galaxy that could fit in a cereal bowl.

There is a kind of freedom in small hours. The world has not yet decided what it wants from you. The phone is silent. The inbox is a quiet meadow rather than a battlefield. You can think in complete sentences, or choose not to think at all and simply observe the steam rising from the cup, bending in a draft you cannot feel.

I used to believe that a meaningful life had to announce itself—applause, promotions, signatures on important documents. But meaning often hides in the unmeasured moments: the way a neighbor’s dog waits at the gate, the sound of rain on a window while you are warm, the patience of a plant that grows one leaf at a time and never asks if it is enough.

Lately I’ve been trying to be softer with myself. Not slower, necessarily, but softer. To meet the day with curiosity instead of a checklist. To let the unfinished poem stay unfinished a little longer. To trust that the light will keep coming, even when the blinds are closed, even when I forget to look.

The coffee is cold now. I drink it anyway.
